directions: Plant bare-root divisions in fall, 4–6 weeks before the ground freezes, setting the pink eyes no more than 1–2 inches below the soil surface in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. European peony is the old-world species behind many historic garden doubles, blooming earlier in spring than the more commonly grown Chinese peony and forming a more compact, rounded clump with deeply cut, dark green leaves. The classic double crimson cultivar 'Rubra Plena' has been passed down in gardens for centuries and remains one of the earliest and longest-lived peonies still commonly grown. Like all peonies it resents being planted too deep or divided too often, and mature clumps can remain productive and largely trouble-free for decades with only an annual fall cleanup of the foliage.

Fernleaf peony is instantly recognizable by its finely dissected, almost feathery foliage that looks more like a carrot top or fennel plant than a typical peony leaf, topped in mid-spring by single or double, deep blood-red cupped flowers held just above the foliage on notably shorter stems than most garden peonies. Native to the steppes of southeastern Europe and the Caucasus, it prefers sharper drainage and leaner soil than the modern Chinese hybrid peonies and resents heavy, wet clay. The foliage remains attractive as a fine-textured accent through much of the growing season even after the brief but showy early bloom has passed.

Commonly nicknamed Molly-the-Witch by gardeners who find its Latin name unpronounceable, this Caucasian species is prized for soft, pale primrose-yellow single flowers that open in very early spring, ahead of nearly every other peony, set against handsome blue-green foliage often tinged reddish-purple at the margins in cool weather. It appreciates light shade from deciduous trees, especially in the hotter part of its range, since the flowers and emerging foliage can be short-lived in strong, direct spring sun. As with other peonies, avoid deep planting and frequent division, and be patient — clumps can take a couple of seasons to settle in before flowering reliably.

planting.note: Plant in spring with the crown set a couple of inches below the soil surface and the base shaded, giving the vine a fence, trellis, or shrub to climb into full sun; blooms entirely on new wood, so it can be cut back hard each late winter.

directions: Plant nursery starts in spring with the crown set a couple of inches below the soil surface and the roots shaded and cool, giving the vine a fence, trellis, or shrub to scramble into in full sun. Viticella clematis is one of the toughest and most disease-resistant of the large clematis groups, producing an abundance of smaller, nodding, four- to six-petaled flowers in shades of purple, magenta, and blue from midsummer into fall on the current season's growth. Because it blooms entirely on new wood, it can be cut back hard to 12–18 inches each late winter, a simple pruning routine that also makes it easy to grow through and rejuvenate an early-blooming shrub or rose. Its resistance to clematis wilt and reliable late-season color have made it a parent species behind many popular modern hybrids, including the 'Ernest Markham' and 'Polish Spirit' cultivars already bred from it.
